newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian rupiah recovers on rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian rupiah recovers on rate hike.

text.p: Indonesia's central bank, Bank Indonesia, raised its short-term interest rates on Tuesday, helping the rupiah to recover from a historic low.
The rupiah bounced back to 2,870 against the dollar from a fresh low of 3,045 after the central bank raised rates for bilateral certificates (SBIs) of maturities between one week and three months.
SBIs, used by the market as a benchmark for interbank rates, are short-term rupiah-denominated obligations issued by the central bank to drain liquidity from the market.
Currency dealers said the hike did not have much impact on the money market because interbank rates were traded higher than SBI rates in the wake of tight liquidity conditions.

However, they said the hike gave a psychological boost to operators. It also reflected the resolve of the central bank to maintain tight monetary policies in an effort to contain currency instability.

The bank said rates for one-week bilateral SBIs were raised to 20 percent from 10.5 percent, two-week to 22 percent from 11, one-month to 30 percent from 11.625 and three-month to 28 percent from 11.5 percent.
The bank maintained overnight SBIs at 15.0 percent, two-to-six day at 16.0, and six-month and one-year at 12.125 and 12.75 percent, respectively.
In the interbank market, one-week money was traded at 70 percent, two-week and one-month at 50 percent and three-month money was at 35/40 percent.
Currency dealers said the sharp difference between the short- and longer-term rates suggested the current instability was temporary.
They said offshore players were looking for some entry level to lock in the attractive yields offered by the rupiah since the morning.

"...things are starting to settle down. Certainly the rupiah at 3,000 is probably the low at the moment, and, to be honest, we are expecting it to start firming up by the end of this week and start to appreciate," Nicholas Bibby, an economist with Chase Manhattan Bank in Hong Kong, told Reuters Financial Television.
Pardy Kendy, chief treasurer of PT Bank Buana Indonesia, said some offshore players were trying to enter the market by selling six-month swaps and establishing short dollar positions.
A swap is a forward rate agreement to exchange one currency for another in the foreign exchange market.
"The rupiah is really undervalued at current levels," Kendy said, adding that the fall of the rupiah since January had made it one of the most undervalued currencies in the region.
The rupiah, which started the year at 2,363, had fallen more than 26 percent if the 3,045 low is taken into account.

Kendy said the Thai baht, whose weakness has triggered speculative attacks on all currencies in the region, had fallen only 25.2 percent since January followed by a 13.65 percent fall in the Philippine peso and 10.67 percent in the Malaysian ringgit.

"I'm surprised to see our rupiah has fallen more than the baht while our economy is in a better shape. The rupiah is really overshooting," he said, adding foreign players seemed to detect the undervaluation and tried to lock in the high yields.

Kendy said offshore fund managers were seen selling dollars in the spot market and placing the rupiah they obtained in six-month swaps, effectively depositing money in rupiah to take advantage of high interest rates.
